title: After September 2001
hookLine: Balbir Singh Sodhi, a Sikh gas station owner in Arizona, is killed in a hate crime

cards: Mesa, Arizona. Saturday, September fifteenth, 2001, four days after the attacks of September eleventh. The whole country is grieving and afraid.

Outside his gas station, a man named Balbir Singh Sodhi is helping a landscaper plant flowers around the sign. Earlier that week, he'd donated to a fund for the victims. He wears a turban and a beard, as many Sikh men do.

teach.b: The man in the truck shot and killed Balbir Singh Sodhi.

That same day he fired at other people he thought looked like the enemy, including a Lebanese American clerk and the home of an Afghan American family. When he was arrested, he said he was standing up for America.
He was convicted of murder. Balbir Singh Sodhi is remembered as one of the first people killed in a hate crime after September eleventh.
He had come to America from Punjab, driven a taxi, saved money with his brothers, and bought that gas station.
In the months and years that followed, many Sikhs in America were attacked, insulted or treated with suspicion, most often because of the turban and beard. Now the hard and important part.

teach.h: NOT A MISTAKE: WRONG FOR ANYONE.
teach.b: It would be easy to say: this was a mistake, he wasn't Muslim. Many Sikhs, and many Sikh organizations, refuse to put it that way. The problem, they say, is not who the attacker got wrong.
It's attacking anyone because of how they look or what they believe. No one deserves that, Muslim, Sikh or anyone else. That teaching is as old as Guru Nanak, who saw the one light in every person.
The Sodhi family answered in the same spirit.

teach.h: A BROTHER WHO TOLD THE STORY.
teach.b: Balbir's brother Rana spent years speaking in schools, churches and community halls, telling his brother's story so people would know their Sikh neighbors.
Ignorance was the soil. Knowing each other is the cure.

how: Sikh Americans remember Balbir Singh Sodhi each September, and many Sikh organizations run school talks, open gurdwara days and langar for neighbors so people come to know one another.

o: a guest welcomed at the langar
a neighbor, the person next door

p: his brother, who told the story
Guru Nanak saw it in every person

s: many Sikhs describe the killing as just a case of mistaken identity
many Sikhs refuse that framing: attacking anyone for how they look is wrong.
Balbir Singh Sodhi had donated to a fund for the victims that week
he gave to help the families of those killed on September 11.
Sikhs in America faced few attacks after 2001
many were attacked, insulted or treated with suspicion, often because of the turban and beard.

games.q: someone tells you the attack was a tragic mistake, because Balbir Singh Sodhi wasn't Muslim. how do many Sikh voices answer?
o: agree: the attacker just got the wrong man.
say no one should be attacked for how they look or believe.
games.why: many Sikhs and Sikh organizations say the wrong was attacking anyone at all, Muslim, Sikh or otherwise.

practice: From everything you've learned on this path, choose one simple true thing about Sikhs: that the turban honors uncut hair, that Sikh means learner, that the langar feeds anyone who walks in.
Say it to yourself in one sentence, the way you'd say it to a friend. Then think of one person who might need to hear it.

wordCard.voice: Guandhi. A neighbor, the person next door — after Balbir Singh Sodhi was killed in a hate crime in Arizona in September 2001, his family worked so neighbors would know each other.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: guandhi, a neighbor; the person next door.

carryVoice: Your line: know your neighbor. Sikh Americans remember Balbir Singh Sodhi each September. Day three hundred twenty.
